brief.subject: Fake debt collectors halted, health data case grows
brief.headline: Court Freezes Phantom Debt Collectors; Five States Join Hims and Hers Privacy Suit
brief.dek: A fake debt collection operation is frozen, a telehealth privacy case expands, and renters and car buyers win against hidden pricing.
brief.lede: At the FTC's request, a federal court froze a debt collection operation accused of pressuring people to pay debts they often did not owe.

sections.heading: Phantom Debt Collectors Frozen
bullets: A federal court temporarily halted the operation and froze its assets after an FTC request.
Collectors allegedly posed as a law firm or claimed ties to attorneys to scare people into paying.
They allegedly threatened to contact employers and family members, a pressure tactic worth recognizing.
Many targeted debts were allegedly not owed at all, so an unexpected demand deserves scrutiny before any payment.

sections.heading: Telehealth Privacy Case Expands
bullets: Five states joined the FTC's lawsuit against telehealth provider Hims and Hers through an amended complaint.
The company allegedly shared sensitive health information with advertising platforms while promising privacy.
It is also accused of misleading users about billing and cancellation, a reason to review recurring charges.

sections.heading: Landlord Pays $49.75 Million
bullets: Progress Residential and owner Pretium Partners will pay $49.75 million to settle FTC and four states' charges.
The single-family rental manager allegedly misled renters with deceptive rental pricing.
The FTC calls it the largest enforcement matter it has taken against a landlord.

sections.heading: Car Dealer Settles Over Ad Prices
bullets: Long Island dealership group Stream Auto Outlet settled FTC claims over misleading advertised prices.
Buyers allegedly paid far more than the advertised figures, a reminder to confirm the full price before signing.
